books.section: Topic 7.4 The Progressives — Roosevelt and the Regulation of Business
The Progressive Era and World War I (1900-1920)

stimulus.source_note: Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20; verbatim excerpt (abridged) from Theodore Roosevelt's 1903 speech, public domain.
stimulus.text:
Paraphrase of Barron's Premium 2027, Chapter 9, and 5 Steps to a 5 2024, Chapter 20: In 1902, anthracite coal miners went on strike, and President Theodore Roosevelt called both sides to the White House, threatening to take over the mines if the owners would not negotiate. The miners won a 10 percent wage increase but not union recognition. Roosevelt called the settlement a 'Square Deal.' He also used the Sherman Antitrust Act against the Northern Securities Company, a railroad holding company, and in 1904 the Supreme Court upheld the breakup.

'We must act upon the motto of all for each and each for all. ... We must see that each is given a square deal, because he is entitled to no more and should receive no less.' — Theodore Roosevelt, speech to farmers in New York, 1903 (abridged)

options.misconception: Roosevelt regulated railroads; he did not break them all up, and the two acts set rules rather than dissolving companies.
Both acts strengthened the federal Interstate Commerce Commission, moving control toward Washington, not back to the states.

options.text: strengthen federal regulation of railroad rates and rebates
let railroads charge whatever rates they wished
options.misconception: Letting railroads charge anything was the unregulated system these acts were written to end.

rationales.A: Neither act dissolved a railroad. Both set rules for rates and rebates under a federal commission.
rationales.B: The acts strengthened the federal Interstate Commerce Commission. Control moved toward Washington, not back to the states.
rationales.C: The Elkins Act attacked rebates to favored customers, and the Hepburn Act gave the Interstate Commerce Commission greater power to set rates. Together they made federal regulation of railroads real.
rationales.D: Free pricing was the system before these acts. Elkins and Hepburn were written to end it.
rationales.general:
1. Name what each act did. Elkins targeted rebates in 1903; Hepburn let the Interstate Commerce Commission set rates in 1906.
2. Add them up. Two laws, both strengthening the same federal regulator, mean stronger federal control of rates and rebates.
3. Rule out the reversals. Breaking up every railroad, returning control to the states, and letting railroads charge anything all point the other way.
Remember: two laws on the same subject add up, so combine their effects before choosing.
